Membrane–actin Brownian ratchet — from boundary baselines to a coupled flexible membrane running

Investigation report · membrane-actin-ratchet · generated 2026-06-08 14:54 UTC · for expert review — results below reflect completed runs.

📋 Executive summary in-progress WORKFLOW-READY, NOT YET VALIDATED. All six studies execute end-to-end and emit observables — the strongest supported conclusion today is that the…

An investigation is a sequence of studies that together answer one research question. This one asks whether a coupled actin (ReaDDy) + membrane (Mem3DG) composite behaves like a real flexible-membrane Brownian ratchet, by comparing three boundary models and stress-testing the coupler that powers the flexible one. It merges two earlier framings — a boundary-condition staircase and a coupling-mechanism deep-dive — into one arc, because the staircase's top rung *is* the coupler the deep-dive validates.

in-progress Current verdict. WORKFLOW-READY, NOT YET VALIDATED. All six studies execute end-to-end and emit observables — the strongest supported conclusion today is that the coupled ReaDDy↔Mem3DG pipeline runs, not that any biological or physical hypothesis has been confirmed. No acceptance test has been evaluated; no benchmark comparison (Peskin 1993, Inoue 2015) has been run. The arc is wired; the verdicts are pending.

Question. Can a particle-based actin Brownian ratchet (ReaDDy) push against a deformable membrane (Mem3DG) through a physically faithful bidirectional coupler, and does increasing boundary realism — fixed wall → rigid movable object → flexible membrane — reproduce the force/velocity signatures that distinguish a flexible-membrane ratchet (Inoue 2015) from the classical rigid-wall regime (Peskin 1993)?

Hypothesis. Boundary realism changes the F-V relationship in a structured, predictable way. (1) The fixed wall reproduces classical Brownian-ratchet kinetics (velocity ≈ 0, contact force accumulates). (2) The rigid movable object introduces a load-dependent stalling regime bounded by Peskin (1993). (3) The flexible Mem3DG membrane qualitatively diverges in the high-load regime because curvature redistributes force across nearby filaments, breaking the per-filament independence the rigid models assume — but only if the actin↔membrane coupler is faithful: equal-and-opposite interface forces (Newton's 3rd law), bounded per-step displacements that preserve mesh quality, and a closed loop that reaches the Inoue-2015 concave→convex transition.

🔬 Scientific argument 4 for · 3 against Boundary realism is the controlling variable for the actin-ratchet F-V relationship, and a faithful Mem3DG↔ReaDDy coupler is necessary to recover the…

Main claim. Boundary realism is the controlling variable for the actin-ratchet F-V relationship, and a faithful Mem3DG↔ReaDDy coupler is necessary to recover the flexible-membrane regime that rigid models cannot produce.

Evidence for

  • [OBSERVED] Fixed and rigid rungs share one actin model; only the barrier changes — a clean controlled comparison, and both run.
  • [OBSERVED] In the fixed rung barrier_velocity holds at ~0 while contact_force accumulates.
  • [OBSERVED] In the flexible rung the vesicle inflates under actin pressure.
  • [INFERRED] Closed-form Peskin (1993) expectations bracket the two rigid rungs — falsifiable, but the comparison has not been run.

Evidence against

  • [OPEN] All acceptance tests are still stubs; no quantitative match has been demonstrated.
  • [OPEN] The concave→convex F-V transition (Inoue 2015) is asserted by construction, not measured — vesicle inflation alone is NOT evidence of ratchet behavior.
  • [OPEN] Newton's-3rd-law balance and mesh-quality preservation are inferred from design, not yet measured.

🧬 Biology — the mechanism this investigation models In a crawling or dividing cell, networks of actin filaments polymerize against the plasma membrane and push it forward. The Brownian-ratchet picture explains how directed…

In a crawling or dividing cell, networks of actin filaments polymerize against the plasma membrane and push it forward. The Brownian-ratchet picture explains how directed motion arises without a molecular motor: thermal fluctuations transiently open a gap between a filament tip and the barrier, a monomer adds into that gap, and the new subunit rectifies the fluctuation into net forward displacement. How much force the network can deliver, and how fast the barrier advances, depends critically on what the filaments are pushing against.

Against a *rigid wall* the problem is classical: each filament ratchets independently and the force/velocity relation follows Peskin's 1993 theory. Let the barrier *move* as a rigid object with drag, and a load-dependent stalling regime appears — the wall advances at a velocity set by the balance between contact force and drag. But a real membrane is neither fixed nor rigid: it *deforms*. Curvature lets the membrane redistribute load across many nearby filaments, relaxing the burden on any single tip and breaking the per-filament independence the rigid theories assume.

Capturing that requires two simulators talking to each other every step: ReaDDy supplies the particle-based actin filaments and their tip dynamics; Mem3DG supplies the deformable, mesh-based membrane. The BrownianRatchetCoupler is the interface — it must translate actin tip forces into membrane vertex loads and feed updated membrane positions back as actin boundary constraints, without violating Newton's third law, without degrading mesh quality, and without breaking ReaDDy's reaction balance. Only when that handshake is faithful does the coupled system reach the diagnostic flexible-membrane signature: the concave→convex force/velocity transition that Inoue et al. (2015) report and that no rigid barrier can reproduce.

This study asks whether in the closed-loop flexible composite, is the force the actin side reports at the interface equal-and-opposite to the force the membrane integrates on its receiving vertices (Newton's 3rd law on the coupling interface)?. Purpose & background (study design)
Question. In the closed-loop flexible composite, is the force the actin side reports at the interface equal-and-opposite to the force the membrane integrates on its receiving vertices (Newton's 3rd law on the coupling interface)?
Mechanism / Model change. BrownianRatchetCoupler reads ReaDDy tip positions, computes per-contact forces using contact_threshold + force_constant, and applies them as osmotic_offset on Mem3DG. The same per-step force scalar must show up in both the actin-side contact_force observable and the membrane-side integrated impulse, up to numerical tolerance.
Expected outcome. Per-step delta(membrane_momentum) ≈ -delta(actin_momentum) within 5%.

This study asks whether does per-step mesh-position feedback from Mem3DG to ReaDDy preserve mesh quality (no vertex inversion or degenerate triangles) and keep tip particles within their box-potential bounds?. Gate decision: In progress. Continue analysing run outcomes.

Purpose & background (study design)
Question. Does per-step mesh-position feedback from Mem3DG to ReaDDy preserve mesh quality (no vertex inversion or degenerate triangles) and keep tip particles within their box-potential bounds?
Mechanism / Model change. After every Mem3DG step the coupler publishes updated wall_radius (planar) or membrane_vertex_positions (spherical) to ReaDDy as the new boundary. Aggressive force_constant or osmotic_force_scale can push the boundary past actin tips in one step, violating bond/box potentials.
Expected outcome. Min triangle area stays above a small positive threshold for the full run; no actin tip overshoots the membrane boundary by more than contact_threshold.

Question. With barrier_kind="rigid_movable", does the wall translate at a velocity proportional to the mean contact force (drag-balance Peskin 1993 setup), and does the stall force remain bounded?

Expected outcome. barrier_velocity stabilizes at a non-zero value over the second half of the run; stall force ≤ Peskin closed-form upper bound at this drag.

Question. With barrier_kind="flexible" (closed-icosphere Mem3DG mesh inside-pushed by bonded actin filaments), does the membrane deform under actin pressure and relax the contact-force burden compared to the rigid_movable rung?
Mechanism / Model change. Spec §2.2 rung 3. This study asks whether does the closed-loop coupled cycle reproduce the Inoue-2015 concave→convex F-V transition as polymerization rate varies — the headline numerical benchmark for a flexible-membrane ratchet (spec §1.2)?. Gate decision: In progress. Continue analysing run outcomes.

Purpose & background (study design)
Question. Does the closed-loop coupled cycle reproduce the Inoue-2015 concave→convex F-V transition as polymerization rate varies — the headline numerical benchmark for a flexible-membrane ratchet (spec §1.2)?
Mechanism / Model change. Sweep growth_rate across the regime where the F-V curve shape flips: at low rates the curve is concave (monomer-delivery limited); at high rates it goes convex (filament-dominated). The flexible barrier is the only rung where this transition can emerge — rigid rungs give a single F-V scatter point per growth_rate, not the transition.
Expected outcome. Across the sweep, the (F, V) scatter cloud is non-monotonic in curvature: concave at low growth_rate, convex at high growth_rate.
